Ancient History.Prehistoric India:
INTRODUCTION
Prehistory refers to the period before the invention of writing. Knowledge about this phase is derived from archaeological sources such as tools, pottery, bones, fossils and cave paintings. It represents the earliest stage of human development and is broadly divided into Paleolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic phases based on the nature of tools and subsistence patterns.

SOURCES OF PREHISTORY
• Archaeological remains such as stone tools, pottery, bones and fossils
• Rock paintings and cave art, especially from Bhimbetka
• Environmental and geological studies
• Absence of written records makes interpretation dependent on material evidence

PALEOLITHIC AGE
This is the earliest phase of human history and is also known as the Old Stone Age. It extended from about 2.5 million years ago to around 10000 BCE and is associated with primitive human existence.

FEATURES
• Use of crude stone tools such as hand axes, cleavers and choppers
• Tools mainly made of quartzite and other hard rocks
• Humans were hunter gatherers and depended on nature
• Nomadic lifestyle with no permanent settlements
• Knowledge of fire in later stages enabled cooking and protection
• Division of Paleolithic into Lower, Middle and Upper phases based on tool development

IMPORTANT SITES
• Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh known for rock shelters and paintings
• Hunsgi in Karnataka
• Kurnool caves in Andhra Pradesh
• Belan Valley in Uttar Pradesh

MESOLITHIC AGE
This is the Middle Stone Age and represents a transitional phase between Paleolithic and Neolithic. It roughly dates from 10000 BCE to 6000 BCE and reflects gradual adaptation to changing climate conditions after the Ice Age.

FEATURES
• Use of microliths or small stone tools often combined with wood and bone
• Beginning of semi permanent settlements
• Domestication of animals such as dog started
• Hunting, fishing and food gathering continued along with early experimentation in cultivation
• Evidence of burials indicating belief systems and social practices
• Increased use of bows and arrows for hunting

IMPORTANT SITES
• Bagor in Rajasthan known for earliest domestication of animals
• Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh
• Langhnaj in Gujarat
• Sarai Nahar Rai in Uttar Pradesh

NEOLITHIC AGE
This is the New Stone Age and marks the beginning of food production. It roughly dates from 6000 BCE to 2000 BCE in India and represents a major transformation in human life.

FEATURES
• Practice of agriculture and domestication of animals such as cattle and sheep
• Use of polished stone tools and improved technology
• Beginning of permanent settlements and village life
• Development of pottery, weaving and storage facilities
• Emergence of social differentiation and community living
• Use of grinding stones and sickles for agriculture

IMPORTANT SITES
• Mehrgarh in present day Pakistan, one of the earliest agricultural settlements
• Burzahom in Kashmir known for pit dwellings
• Chirand in Bihar
• Hallur in Karnataka

SIGNIFICANCE
• Transition from food gathering to food production which is known as Neolithic Revolution
• Foundation for settled life and development of villages
• Beginning of technological advancements such as pottery and tool making
• Development of social organisation and early cultural practices
• Basis for the emergence of later civilizations like the Indus Valley Civilization

IMPORTANT POINTS
• Bhimbetka rock shelters are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and provide evidence of continuous human habitation
• Paleolithic tools are mostly made of unpolished stones whereas Neolithic tools are polished
• Mesolithic phase is marked by microlithic tools and transitional economy
• Mehrgarh provides earliest evidence of agriculture and domestication in the Indian subcontinent

PYQ FOCUS AREAS
• Difference between Paleolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic phases
• Important archaeological sites and their features
• Transition from hunting gathering to agriculture
• Tool types and technological changes

CONCLUSION
Prehistoric India laid the foundation for later developments in human civilization. The gradual transition from primitive hunting gathering societies to settled agricultural communities represents one of the most significant transformations in human history and set the stage for urban civilizations.
